Essential expenses are taking up an increasing portion of US household spending:

Healthcare, housing, utilities, gasoline, financial services, and insurance now account for 45.6% of total US consumer expenditures, near the highest proportion on record.

Over the last 4 years, this figure has risen +1.8 percentage points from its lowest level since 2004.

By comparison, these essential expenses represented a record 46.5% in 2010, following the 2008 Financial Crisis.

Meanwhile, between the 1960s and the 1980s, this proportion never exceeded 40%.

In 1959, these categories accounted for less than 30% of total consumer expenditures.

Mandatory spending is eating up a growing portion of US household budgets.

How I trade is simple -- although to each element of "simple" I have many rules (that I follow)
-Classical chart patterns (horizontal ones) 8 to 26 weeks in length is my swing zone
-Buy or sell an adjusted ATR breakout
-Please stops to disallow the market to dig too deeply in my pockets
-Limit risk per trade to 7/10th of 1% of total nominal capital
-Use open orders
-Move protective stops to B/E as soon as reasonable
-Take partial profits if profit of tranche > 50 basis points
-Take profit at targets
-Use 8 DMA to manage trade
I usually assume that I will get two to three good signals in any given market each year

US hiring plans are picking up as seasonal demand accelerates:

US-based employers announced plans to hire 444,692 workers in October, up +57% YoY and the highest October total since at least 2009.

Technology led with 300,252 announced positions, followed by Transportation at 100,000, and Retail at 13,300.

Year-to-date hiring plans are up +34% YoY, to 655,304 workers.

Meanwhile, seasonal hiring announcements jumped +26% YoY, to 470,400, but remained 29% below the 660,150 recorded in 2024.

Seasonal positions now account for 72% of all hiring plans in 2026 and nearly 60% of the increase from last year.

Seasonal hiring is gaining momentum.

BREAKING: Student loan serious delinquencies increased +0.3 percentage points in Q3 2026, to 10.9%, the highest percentage since Q4 2019.

This marks the 4th consecutive quarterly increase, with a cumulative gain of +1.5 percentage points.

Auto loan 90+ day serious delinquencies rose +0.2 percentage points, to 5.7%, their highest level on record.

By comparison, the post-2008 Financial Crisis peak in this metric stood at 5.3% in Q4 2010.

Meanwhile, credit card 90+ day delinquencies stood at 12.9%, the 2nd-highest level since Q1 2011.

US households are falling further behind on their debt payments.

Value stocks are making a historic comeback:

The Russell 1000 Value Index is outperforming the Russell 1000 Growth Index by 27.7 percentage points so far in 2026, its strongest relative performance since 2000.

The Russell 1000 Value Index includes stocks across multiple sectors, including healthcare, industrials, consumer staples, and utilities.

This marks a sharp reversal after growth stocks outperformed value by 31.2 percentage points in 2023, 19.0 percentage points in 2024, and 2.7 percentage points in 2025.

By comparison, during the 2022 bear market, value stocks outperformed growth by 21.6 percentage points.

This comes as the Russell 1000 Value Index is up +24.8% year-to-date, while the Russell 1000 Growth Index is down -2.9% over the same period.

Market dynamics are rapidly shifting.

The new rules aim to prevent China and others subject to US export restrictions from circumventing existing controls by accessing American AI technology through cloud computing services.

Prior to this, a loophole allowed foreign entities to access advanced US computing capabilities without physically importing restricted chips.

More AI regulation is on the way.
